name: The Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
statement: Two strangers agree on a shared secret over an open channel that an eavesdropper cannot reconstruct.
statementAccent: agree on a shared secret over an open channel
meaning: The Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a method that allows two parties, who have no prior shared secret and are communicating over an insecure, public channel, to jointly establish a shared secret key. That shared key can then be used with a fast symmetric cipher to encrypt their subsequent communication. It was one of the first public-key protocols and is a foundational method for key exchange. In its classic modular-arithmetic form, the two parties, conventionally called Alice and Bob, first publicly agree on a large prime number p and a base, or generator, g. Each then chooses a secret private number: Alice picks a, Bob picks b. Alice computes and sends g raised to the power a, modulo p; Bob computes and sends g raised to the power b, modulo p. Each then raises the value received from the other to their own secret exponent: Alice computes Bob's value to the power a, and Bob computes Alice's value to the power b, and both arrive at the same number, g raised to the power a times b, modulo p, which becomes their shared secret. An eavesdropper who observes g, p, and the two exchanged values cannot feasibly compute the shared secret, because doing so requires solving the discrete logarithm problem. The protocol was published in 1976 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, building on ideas of Ralph Merkle; an equivalent scheme had been developed secretly by Malcolm Williamson at GCHQ around 1974, declassified in 1997. Diffie-Hellman remains central to internet security.
mechanism: The Diffie-Hellman key exchange lets two parties construct a common secret from separately held private numbers, using the one-way behaviour of modular exponentiation. The parties begin by agreeing, in the open, on a large prime p and a generator g modulo p; these are public and may be known to anyone, including an adversary. Each party then privately selects a secret exponent, Alice choosing a and Bob choosing b, and computes a public value by raising g to that exponent modulo p: Alice sends g to the a mod p, Bob sends g to the b mod p. The crucial algebraic fact is that exponentiation commutes: when Alice raises Bob's value to her secret, she computes g to the b, all to the a, and when Bob raises Alice's value to his secret, he computes g to the a, all to the b, and both equal g to the a times b modulo p. So without ever transmitting their private exponents, the two parties compute the same shared secret. An eavesdropper sees g, p, g to the a, and g to the b, but to recover the secret must find a or b from g to that power, which is the discrete logarithm problem, believed computationally infeasible for suitable large parameters; the closely related computational Diffie-Hellman problem is the exact task the eavesdropper faces. The scheme is often explained by an analogy of mixing paint colours, where mixing is easy but unmixing is hard. Diffie-Hellman by itself provides no authentication, so it is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack unless combined with a means of verifying identities, and its widely used elliptic-curve variant, ECDH, replaces modular arithmetic with elliptic-curve operations for stronger security at smaller key sizes.

variants.name: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman
variants.text: Using fresh temporary keys per session provides forward secrecy, protecting past traffic if a long-term key leaks.

whyItMatters: The Diffie-Hellman key exchange is one of the founding achievements of modern cryptography, the first published method by which two parties could establish a shared secret over an open channel without ever having met, and it remains in constant use protecting internet communication today. Its introduction in 1976, in Diffie and Hellman's paper that also launched public-key cryptography, solved a problem that had stymied cryptographers for centuries, how to agree on a secret key without a secure channel to share it, and it did so with an idea of remarkable simplicity and beauty grounded in modular arithmetic and the hardness of the discrete logarithm. Diffie-Hellman is embedded throughout the systems that secure daily life: it is used in TLS and HTTPS, in virtual private networks, in SSH, and in secure messaging apps like Signal, and its ephemeral variants provide forward secrecy, ensuring that recorded traffic stays safe even if long-term keys are later compromised. Its elliptic-curve form, ECDH, is the common modern choice, offering strong security with small keys. The protocol's history, publicly pioneered by Diffie and Hellman with Merkle and independently discovered in secret at GCHQ, and honored with the 2015 Turing Award, marks it as a landmark. As the method that lets strangers agree on a shared secret in the open, the Diffie-Hellman key exchange is indispensable to secure communication.

limits: The Diffie-Hellman key exchange is elegant but has limits that reward care. By itself it provides no authentication: it establishes a shared secret but does not verify who is at the other end, so it is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack, in which an adversary interposes and exchanges keys separately with each party, unless it is combined with signatures or certificates that authenticate identities. Its security rests on the assumed hardness of the discrete logarithm and the related computational Diffie-Hellman problem, which are believed but not proven hard and which a large enough quantum computer could break, motivating post-quantum key exchange. Parameters must be chosen carefully: weak or small primes, poorly chosen generators, or reused ephemeral keys have led to real attacks, and the elliptic-curve variant ECDH is now generally preferred. Some historical details reward care: the protocol was published by Diffie and Hellman in 1976, building on Merkle's work, with Hellman later suggesting the name Diffie-Hellman-Merkle; an equivalent scheme was developed secretly by Malcolm Williamson at GCHQ around 1974, part of GCHQ work declassified in 1997. So Diffie-Hellman robustly establishes a shared secret over an open channel, understood as an unauthenticated protocol whose security is conjectural and whose parameters must be chosen with care.
misreadings: Diffie-Hellman does not authenticate the parties; without added verification it is open to a man-in-the-middle attack. Its security is not proven but rests on the discrete logarithm being hard, which quantum computers threaten. And it establishes a shared secret, not encryption itself, so treating the bare protocol as authenticated, as unconditionally secure, or as an encryption scheme rather than a key exchange, misreads it.
origin: The key-exchange protocol published by Diffie and Hellman in 1976, and secretly devised by Williamson at GCHQ around 1974, letting two parties establish a shared secret over an open channel via the hardness of the discrete logarithm.
